lawyer:
Azizul Haque with Abu Ferdous, Md. Sayeed, Advocates ------ For Appellants. 
Sultan Ahmed, D.A.G. with Md. Marfat Ali, Md. Altafur Rahman, & Malik Syed Ahmed, Advocates ------ For the State.
parties:
Mahitullah Pk and Others ------ Petitioner
Vs.
The State ------ Respondent
full_judgment: 5. Section 268 of the old Code of Criminal Procedure contemplates all trial before a court of Sessions either by jury or with the aid of assessors. In the present case, after the commitment by the Magistrate concerned the records were sent to the court of sessions on 15-6-77. While the records were pending in the court of sessions, the Law Reforms Ordinance, 1978 (XLIX) came into being on 1-6-79 by virtue of which the Criminal Procedure for trial with the aid of assessors was done away with. The trial before the Sessions Judge started in the case on 16-3-1981 after framing of the charge and after the accused persons pleaded not guilty with the charge and claimed to be tried. According to Mr. Azizul Haque, section 4 of the Law Reforms Ordinance contemplates that the trial should be held according to the old Code of Criminal Procedure as if no amendment has been made and in that view he argues that the case being a pending one should be tried with the aid of assessors. In this case, it is not disputed that the records were transmitted to the court of sessions on 15-6-77 and the Law Reforms Ordinance came into being on 1-6-79. The material question for consideration is when actually the trial started. By mere pendency of the case before the Sessions Judge, it cannot be said that the trial had actually started. The trial of the sessions case starts when the accused is formally charged by the Sessions Judge and when he pleads not guilty than the Sessions Judge proceeds to carry on with the trial. In this case from the order-sheet it appears that on 16-3-81 the trial started and before that the Law Reforms Ordinance came into existence on 1-6-79. The trial of session’s case commences when the accused is brought before the court to stand his trial and at that time the trial commences. The deleted section 271 of the Code of Criminal Procedure reads as follows:—(1) When the court is ready to commence the trial, the accused shall appear or be brought before it and the charge shall be read out in court and explained to him, and he shall be asked whether he is guilty of the offence charged, or claims to be tried. Thus according to section 271(1) of the old Code of Criminal Procedure a trial really commences when the formality of section 271(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure is followed. Thus it cannot be said that the trial started before this procedure is followed. It can at best be said that the session’s case was pending before the Sessions Judge who actually took up the trial nearly two years of the promulgation of Law Reforms Ordinance, 1978. Language of section 4 of the Law Reforms Ordinance also speaks that any appeal, application, trial, enquiry or investigation which was pending immediately before such amendment takes effect shall be contained, held, made or disposed of in accordance with the provision of the said Code as was in force before such amendment as if no such amendment has been made. Thus it is also clear from the language that if the trial would have started earlier then of course this argument of the learned Advocate for the appellants would have been available. But here the trial commenced after about two years of the promulgation of the ordinance and as such it cannot be said that the trial has been vitiated for not complying with the old provision of section 268 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. In this connection it will not be out of place to refer section 272 of the old Code of Criminal Procedure which provides that the assessors come on the picture only if the accused refused to plead or pleads not guilty or claims to be tried. Till the trial commences within the meaning of section 271 of the Code no vested right accrues to the accused to be tried according to the procedure laid down under the Code. Further presence or absence of assessors relates to the mode of trial and to the constitution of the court and in the present case this objection was also not taken at the trial stage. The appellants faced the trial and after conviction in the trial they preferred this appeal and at the final hearing this objection have been taken by the learned advocate for the appellants. In this connection, it may be pointed out that the Law Reforms Ordinance, 1978 came into being to amend certain law for the purpose of quick and easy dispensation of justice by providing some amendments in the procedural system. Thus we find that the legislature in the meanwhile has changed the old procedure Code and has introduced certain amendments and the new procedure should be made applicable to the trial. We have also found out earlier that the trial really commenced on 16-3-81 long after promulgation of Law Reforms Ordinance, 1978 on 1-6-78 and as such the contention of the learned Advocate for the appellants that the trial is vitiated by the failure for not calling assessors for aiding at the trial has got no substance. Mr. Azizul Haque has submitted two decisions for our consideration. He has cited a case reported in 6 DLR Dacca 647, that was a case under section 281 of the old Code and the decision speaks that the Court constituted with less than 3 assessors or with more than 4 assessors would be illegal. This decision has got no application to the facts of the present case. The learned advocate has cited a decision reported in 10 DLR 61. That is a case which deals with misjoinder of both persons and offences under section 239(d) of the Code of Criminal Procedure which seriously vitiates the trial. That case we are afraid has got no manner of application with the present case with which we are dealing. The learned Deputy Attorney General appearing for, the State cited a decision reported in 19 DLR (S.C) 241. This is a case which is squarely on the point. In that case the accused was committed to the court of sessions for trial on 6.6.63 and the trial commenced with the aid of assessors. By the Provincial Amendment Act (West Pakistan Act XVII of 1964) which came into effect on           1-4-64 the procedure for trial with assessors was done away with. In that case it was contended that the accused had a vested right to be tried with the aid of assessors when it was committed on 6-6-63 when the amending law did not come into force. In that case their Lordships of the Supreme Court considered at length section 271 and 272 of the Code of Criminal Procedure read with section 537 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and held that the objection is not sustainable.
